## Motivation

Noise-prediction diffusion learns how corruption relates to clean examples and uses a sampler to generate from noise.
Here $A$ is a demonstrated [action chunk]{.term key="action-chunk"}, $o$ is its observation condition, and $k$ indexes the amount of corruption.
The question is how a model trained against known random noise can generate an action when the clean answer is unavailable.

## What noise prediction learns {#diffusion}

For one common noise-prediction formulation, training constructs

$$
  A_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\,A
  +\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\epsilon,
$$

where $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ is [Gaussian noise]{.term key="gaussian-distribution"} and the fixed schedule $\bar\alpha_k$ decreases as corruption increases.
The network receives $(A_k,o,k)$ and predicts $\hat\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(A_k,o,k)$.
Its simplified training objective is

$$
  L_{\mathrm{noise}}
  =\mathbb E[\|\hat\epsilon-\epsilon\|^2].
$$

Here, the known sampled noise supplies supervision.
The clean demonstration constructs the corrupted training input; it is not a required inference input.
This is the noise-prediction formulation of [DDPM, Sections 3.2 and 3.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239), with observation conditioning added for a policy.

The ideal squared-error predictor is

$$
  \epsilon^*(A_k,o,k)
  =\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid A_k,o,k].
$$

This is a [conditional expectation]{.term key="conditional-expectation"}: an average over noise values compatible with the supplied inputs.
The equality describes the population squared-error optimum when the relevant second moments are finite and the predictor is unrestricted; a trained finite network only approximates it.
Its conditioning includes the location of the current noisy sample, so it defines a field across noisy action space instead of one final answer for an observation.

At inference, a sampler starts with noise and repeatedly uses the trained network to update the sample.
A scheduler supplies the update coefficients and, for a stochastic sampler, any additional random noise.
There is no stored clean target being subtracted at inference.
Only the final clean prediction is eligible for execution, as detailed in [Diffusion Policy](../../literature-review/action/diffusion-policy.qmd).

## Example and conditions of use

Suppose demonstrations reach around either side of an obstacle.
A direct action predictor sees the observation and must return one chunk, whereas the diffusion predictor also sees the current noisy candidate and its noise level.
Two different noisy candidates can therefore receive different predictions under the same observation; this is the relevant difference in their inputs, not the disappearance of conditional averaging.

The displayed construction assumes additive Gaussian corruption and a schedule with $0\leq\bar\alpha_k\leq1$.
The noise has the same shape as the action chunk, and generation must supply the observation, noise-level convention, and normalisation expected during training.
The sampler and network together determine the generated distribution; the MSE objective alone does not specify the reverse updates.
Neither finite-step sampling nor a low training loss guarantees that all demonstrated strategies are reproduced.

## Compare the targets {#targets}

Direct squared-error action prediction learns a [conditional mean of actions](loss.qmd#conditional-mean).
The diffusion objective instead conditions on the current noisy sample as well as the observation and noise level.
These conditional averages are functions of different inputs and predict different quantities.
[Flow matching](flow-matching.qmd) uses another local target, a velocity along a constructed probability path.
[Generative sampling](../robotics/generative-sampling.qmd) separates the learned field from the random draws and numerical updates used to generate an output.

## References

[Ho et al., Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, §§3.2–3.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239) gives the corruption process and simplified noise-prediction objective.
[Chi et al., Diffusion Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04137) applies conditional denoising to robot action sequences.
